Transporting RD and BD by rail can offer environmental advantages as well as the ability to efficiently transport large volumes of fuels with ease (Union Pacific, 2022a). In addition, transporting RD and BD via rail provides the opportunity to take advantage of financial incentives available in states like California, Oregon, and Washington (Union Pacific, 2022b). 5.3.2 Environmental Benefits and Tradeoffs To assess the potential benefits and tradeoffs of scaling up biofuel use in the rail sector, we considered three diesel-biofuel blending cases: RD100, BD100, and BD20+RD80. Although RD100 and BD20+RD80 can serve as a drop-in replacement for diesel, BD100 would require engine modifications or fuel additives. All three of these biofuel blending cases substantially reduced rail-sector emissions compared to conventional diesel (Figure 5-18). CO e emissions 2 decreased by 32.9, 29.7, and 33.5 million MT in the RD100, BD100, and BD20+RD80 cases, respectively. This is equivalent to reductions of 76%, 69%, and 77% compared to conventional diesel use. Emissions decreased more in the RD100 and BD20+RD80 cases compared to the BD100 case. This is because, for these two cases, RD is produced from different feedstocks and pathways with various lifecycle CO e emissions impacts. RD from swine manure and sewage sludge have 2 negative lifecycle CO e emissions, which contributes to the reduction in overall emissions 2 compared to the BD case. However, the limited supply of these resources limits their scalability potential. Overall, the BD20+RD80 case has the lowest lifecycle CO e emissions. BD from soybeans has 2 lower lifecycle CI than RD from soybeans (Figure 2-5). Because the WTP 10 PM emission intensities of most biofuel pathways are higher than those for diesel, the life cycle PM emissions are also higher.
